It struck me that one of the handicaps in that kind of settlement was the lack of contact with the outside world after the sun went down. During the daytime they could at least see a lot and they were kept occupied, but at night in the sections I visited the people did not have radios, and when I came back to Toronto I asked the department what they could do to improve conditions along that line. Of course unless an electric wire was strung along the road they could not have electric radios. They might have been able to use battery radios, but the families that went north took little furniture with them, and whether or not they had radios before I do not know. But certain of these settlers were backed up by the different communities from which they left to go north. I think that East York, for instance, and some of the municipalities around there undertook to try to make conditions better for those who went from their community. Quite a number of people in the south could perhaps spare a radio for some family in the north. Certainly any family that goes to northern Ontario should be assisted in every possible way, and if after three years they still need further assistance I should be glad to support a vote which the minister might ask for to assist until these people really get on their feet. They all had small houses and were clearing small farms, and an occasional one, but not all of them, had a cow. In one community I visited there was. only one horse for seven families. There was not such a lot to do, of course, because at the outset they had only from one to five acres cleared, and perhaps one horse could take care of seven families.
Those who have to do with this kind of settlement should keep in close touch with the settlers, because they are worthy people, and even after the three years have expired every effort should be made to keep them going. Many of them will make good. I found some of them working on the roads. They would clear what land they could, and then the Ontario government would give them work to do on the main roads. If they got paid for that, it would be of some assistance in providing income. Certainly I believe that both governments and all those connected with such settlement should make every effort to provide some kind of work by which the settlers can get a little ready money, besides having the opportunity to raise vegetables and whatever else they may require. I can say for northern Ontario that I never saw better patches of potatoes than I saw up there, and the same with other vegetables.
I was surprised at the tremendous growth, because my impression before going north 
had been that the season was so short that vegetables that grow so prolifically in southern Ontario would not mature up there, but the settlers told me that while their season * was shorter ^ the growing season was hotter, and they did not anticipate any trouble in that regard. I know what trouble the minister and the department must have in doing justice to a scheme of this land, but certainly anything that the department feels it is necessary to do to help out these settlers should be done.

I would just like to say that in Fort William several rooms in the schools had to be closed because of this movement towards the land. I know of only one family that had to come back. I could give you a picture of a home that I did not have afternoon tea in but something better, and not home brew. This family had been on relief in the city of Fort William, but they went on the land. The father was delicate. Now they would not move back because they say they have what firewood they need, and all the milk they need; they grow their own vegetables, keep their own fowl and have all the eggs they need. They get an odd job that brings them in a little cash to buy what they call luxuries. These people would not go back to the city. Of course, it depends not so much upon the man as upon the wife who goes out into these settlements, and I pay this tribute to some of them who went out and slaved and self-sacrificed in order to make good. That is the kind of spirit that made Canada great in its early days.
Progress reported.
